To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the risk of dying from any cause is higher in the first three days and first week of life for newborns in Nigeria, and that risk factors for dying from any cause, birth injury/birth-asphyxia, and neonatal infections are different.

the risk of death from birth injury/bih asphyxia was 1.8 times higher among neonates from households that did not have electricity, and 1.7 times higher for neonates whose mothers were illiterate compared to neonates whose mothers had secondary education or higher.

1) the majority of neonatal deaths occur during the first week, 2) most deaths due to BIBAs and neonatal infections occur during the first 24 h of life, and 3) the neonatal mortality hazard ratio of newborns with a severe illness at birth onset was higher on any particular day compared to those who were not sick at birth.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the temporal distribution of neonatal mortality and the role of socioeconomic and cultural factors in the survival time of newborns in Nigeria.
the temporal distribution of mortality and the risk factors that influence it among newborns.

understanding how the timing of neonatal death is associated with a range of factors, including socioeconomic and demographic characteristics, maternal behaviors, and the context in which newborns die.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the risk factors for neonatal deaths in Nigeria are complex.
a large proportion of neonatal deaths in Nigeria occur in the first 7 days of life and that a substantial proportion of these occur in the first day of life.

the findings of the current study suggest that the neonates who were born to the poor households with no electricity, who had a severe neonatal illness at onset, who did not receive any antenatal care, or who had an illness in the first week after birth were at higher risks of dying in the first week, especially during the first day of life.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the neonatal period in Nigeria is characterized by a high mortality rate, with most of the deaths occurring in the first week.
the neonatal mortality hazard is highest during the first day of life and that neonates who have a severe illness at birth are at a significantly higher risk of dying.
newborn deaths in Nigeria were mostly concentrated in the first week, with the first day of life being particularly vulnerable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
neonatal deaths in Nigeria are concentrated in the first week and the first day of life.
the neonatal mortality rate is not an appropriate measure of neonatal mortality in Nigeria and other similar countries.
the time-to-death analysis is a useful tool for understanding the temporal distribution of neonatal deaths and the factors that contribute to it.
